judgeRationales.scenarioName: ASP.NET Core app with DI validation, forwarded headers, and HttpClientFactory casting
judgeRationales.rationale: B is modestly better because it covers the important new Development DI validation issue that A misses and adopts a safer framing for restoring header diagnostics. Neither fully delivers the exact scoped-into-singleton correction in its final response, and both otherwise cover the main proxy, HttpClient handler, logging, and watch concerns comparably.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: App with JsonDocument null deserialization and BinaryFormatter fallback
judgeRationales.rationale: A delivers a net9.0 project with all three cited breaking changes addressed and reports a clean build. B identifies the issues and partially edits the code, but explicitly stops before resolving BinaryFormatter and never obtains a clean final build, so it does not fulfill the migration task.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: App with empty environment variables, ZIP encoding, and keyed DI services
judgeRationales.rationale: B catches the crucial empty-environment-variable breaking change while A directly contradicts it. Both are comparable on ZIP and keyed DI; B also reports a verified clean net9.0 build, whereas A leaves the project failing to build. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: C# 13 compiler breaking changes — InlineArray on record, iterator safe context, collection expressions
judgeRationales.rationale: A is correct and direct on all three migration breaks, including the important concrete overload-resolution outcome. B has the right fixes overall but materially muddies the resolver diagnosis and presents a distracting malformed intermediate example.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: CI pipeline with Terminal Logger parsing and version constraints
judgeRationales.rationale: B covers two important .NET 9 CI migration issues that A entirely misses (Terminal Logger and workload output) while matching A on the SDK, VS, and obsolete-TFM findings. Both miss the requested dotnet-watch/Hot Reload issue. A does add the valuable observation that the captured build exit code is ignored, whereas B does not, so B's overall advantage is limited rather than large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Containerized app with env var precedence reversal and zlib removal
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses contain the same major correctness failure about the unsupported ThreadPool environment variable, yielding the wrong effective MinThreads and remediation. A is modestly better overall because its core precedence narrative and GC impact are less hedged and more accurate than B's misleading assertion that the GC environment values likely already applied in .NET 8. B's extra CET and conversion discussion does not repair the key deployment error.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Containerized app with zlib dependency and runtime configuration
judgeRationales.rationale: A is more complete and actionable, notably handling global.json and giving a concrete .NET Monitor replacement. However, both share the major ThreadPool configuration error, so A's overall advantage is limited rather than large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: EF Core Cosmos DB app with discriminator and sync I/O
judgeRationales.rationale: A is more complete for the actual legacy-data migration: most importantly, it supplies the correct discriminator-in-JSON-id compatibility configuration and also discusses the separate shadow-id mapping change. B has the same major observations but its proposed id API/signature undermines an exact, deployable fix.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: EF Core Cosmos DB app with existing documents and composite id format
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: EF Core app with migration patterns and Cosmos DB discriminator
judgeRationales.rationale: Both complete the core app migration and satisfy every required breaking-change item. A is slightly stronger overall because its Cosmos id compatibility guidance uses the EF Core 9 HasDiscriminatorInJsonId API and it also notes the Cosmos raw-SQL projection change. B usefully adds the HasIndex break, but its HasRootDiscriminatorInJsonId(true) recommendation is less clearly appropriate for EF Core 9.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Library with String.Trim span overload, keyed services, and InlineArray
judgeRationales.rationale: B covers all four required breaking changes, including the UserAgent nullability change that A misses, and reports a clean build. A is somewhat more decisive and precise on the keyed DI fix, but that does not offset omitting a required migration issue.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: WinForms app with custom UserControls and PictureBox URL loading
judgeRationales.rationale: The substantive migration coverage is nearly identical and both miss the CET point. A is slightly stronger because it gives the exact StatusStrip default change and accurately reports that the original project still has a pre-existing missing-entry-point build failure. B's claim of a verified zero-error build is misleading because it achieved that only by overriding OutputType to Library rather than building the project as configured.

Its broad claim that every item is an ASPDEPR warning is imprecise (the cookie behavior is not), but it immediately distinguishes that behavior and does not undermine the central guidance. B has a consequential incorrect recommendation for NSwag/client generation and a likely incorrect property casing.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: App using SslStream properties and SystemEvents
judgeRationales.rationale: B correctly answers all four requested migration diagnostics. A is otherwise strong and provides useful extra context, but its incorrect XSLT conclusion leaves one of the four central requested items wrong.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Blazor WASM app with generic math shift masking and tar operations
judgeRationales.rationale: B addresses every requested compatibility issue and supplies the required trimming/HTTP3 fix. A is otherwise solid on generic shifts, async reads, and TAR timestamps, but its incorrect HTTP/3/trimming guidance is a material omission that could leave the application broken.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: C# 14 compiler breaking changes — field keyword, extension keyword, disposal
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses cover all four requested migration issues and fixes. B is marginally better because it gives the required definite post-disposal behavior rather than qualifying it with unsupported alternative outcomes.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Console app with System.Linq.Async, SIGTERM, and BufferedStream
judgeRationales.rationale: B covers all four requested migration impacts, especially the critical SIGTERM change. A's direct contradiction on SIGTERM makes its otherwise useful answer unsafe for this Docker console application.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Containerized single-file app with P/Invoke and IDispatchEx
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more directly actionable and fully covers the two deployment/interop changes central to the prompt: adding AssemblyDirectory for the single-file P/Invoke and restoring NativeAOT rpath explicitly. A covers several items well but is incomplete and less precise on those two points.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Cryptography app with OpenSSL, X.509, and Rfc2898DeriveBytes
judgeRationales.rationale: B covers every required migration item, most importantly the obsolete Rfc2898DeriveBytes constructors and Pbkdf2 replacement. A's affirmative claim that this constructor has no relevant breaking change is a significant migration error. B has a minor dubious environment-variable aside and omits the ICU rename, but its core requested guidance is substantially more correct. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: EF Core app with Azure SQL JSON columns and parameterized collections
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are concise, actionable, and cover all three directly applicable breaking changes correctly. B is marginally stronger because it states the important compatibility-level condition on the Azure SQL json mapping, avoiding an overbroad claim.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: EF Core app with dynamic ExecuteUpdate and complex types
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers cover all requested EF Core 10 breaks and provide usable fixes. B has the important API signature detail right for ExecuteUpdateAsync (Action rather than Func); A is somewhat clearer on the concrete complex-column collision behavior, but its delegate-type claim is a real compile-time API inaccuracy.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Expression tree code broken by C# 14 span overload resolution
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: JSON polymorphism with conflicting property names and XmlSerializer
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly cover the JSON, XmlSerializer, and MailAddress changes. B alone gets the URI breaking change right, while A reverses it; this is an important but one-of-four-topic error, making B overall slightly better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Library with NuGet auditing, transitive deps, and InlineArray
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers cover every requested migration issue accurately at a high level. B is more precise on the disallowed InlineArray layout and Stem fix, and avoids A's misleading qualification and unnecessary configuration advice.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: SDK and NuGet obscure tooling changes
judgeRationales.rationale: B accurately covers all seven requested migration changes and gives the key concrete SLNX and HTTP/retry guidance. A gets several basics right but is materially wrong on direct-reference pruning semantics and the HTTP/retry change, and fails to provide the required `--format sln` fix.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: SQLite app with DateTimeOffset timezone handling
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly and accurately covers each of the three specified .NET 10 changes and the opt-out switch. A gets the offset-less TEXT change and switch right but omits the REAL write conversion, muddles the GetDateTime behavior, and includes a misleading claim about cross-machine effects.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: WinForms and WPF desktop app with System.Drawing and DynamicResource
judgeRationales.rationale: B addresses the key prescribed migration fixes, especially type ambiguity and removal of empty XAML definitions. A has major incorrect substitutions and inaccurate claims, despite correctly covering the DynamicResource and StatusStrip topics.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Worker service with config null array binding and ProviderAlias assembly change
judgeRationales.rationale: B correctly answers all five migration concerns. A has material factual errors on ProviderAlias assembly-qualified resolution and keyed-service AnyKey behavior, two of the user's specific compatibility questions. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Blocking WaitHandle with Thread.Interrupt
judgeRationales.rationale: A provides the more idiomatic and generally safer .NET 8 producer/consumer redesign, eliminating the manual event/queue signaling race and covering useful migration pitfalls. B is stronger on the explicitly requested WaitAny pattern and candid about cooperative shutdown, but its retained ManualResetEventSlim scheme can still lose a producer signal, and it disposes the CTS even after a timed-out Join while the worker may remain alive. A's claimed bounded StopAsync timeout is incomplete for a synchronous non-cooperative Handle, preventing a larger advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: ASP.NET Core app with OpenAPI customizations and Blazor Virtualize
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are correct and cover both rubric points accurately. A adds concrete, source-grounded code examples for the OpenAPI v3 migration (IOpenApiMediaType, OpenApiXml.NodeType) making it more actionable, while B is more concise with a useful caveat about unaffected apps. A's added specificity gives it a slight edge; both are otherwise equivalent in quality on the required points.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: BackgroundService exceptions and ZipArchive CRC32 validation
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identify the two breaking changes and give correct mitigation advice, satisfying both rubric criteria. A is more thorough and precise: it addresses the user's specific reliance on 'silent ignoring' by explaining the Ignore option still works but no longer restarts the worker, distinguishes where CRC validation and eager loading errors occur, notes the lack of a compatibility switch, and provides authoritative doc links plus preview-status caveat. A was derived from deep research of actual runtime source/PRs, while B leaned on a bundled skill reference. B is accurate and concise but slightly less complete and slightly mischaracterizes the CreateAsync change as primarily a memory concern. The gap is modest since both cover the core rubric points.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Basic TFM update with Docker and global.json
judgeRationales.rationale: Both give solid migration guidance covering all four files. A's key advantage is factual accuracy verified against live sources: it confirmed the actual latest preview (preview.7) and that 11.0 Docker tags do NOT exist yet (only 11.0-preview), so B's generic 11.0 image tags would fail to pull and its preview.3 SDK version is stale. B is stronger on package-reference guidance and includes helpful breaking-change notes and dotnet test/CI advice (though B's skill reference file reads all failed, so its breaking-change specifics are somewhat unverified). On balance, A's correctness on the concrete, actionable version pins outweighs B's better package-reference and breaking-change coverage, making A slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: C# 15 compiler breaking changes — Span safe-context, nameof, with()
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identify all three breaking changes and give the core fixes. Response A is more thorough, provides correct and self-consistent code (whereas Response B's Span fix retains 'scoped Span<int> results' while assigning an int[] and calling ToArray(), which is internally inconsistent and wouldn't compile), and cites diagnostics. Response B is much more concise and used the migration skill, but its main Span fix is flawed. A is slightly better overall due to correctness.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: C# 15 dynamic operator and ref readonly delegate issues
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Console app with compression and TAR operations
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly cover all four rubric criteria with sound migration advice, so they tie on the first two. Response A is more thorough and precise on the ZipArchive nuance (contents not eagerly decompressed) and on MemoryStream (identifying that the preview capacity limit was reverted), backed by verification against live docs and source. Response B is efficient and correct but less nuanced. A is slightly better overall due to greater accuracy and depth on the harder-to-verify items.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: App with JsonDocument null deserialization and BinaryFormatter fallback
judgeRationales.rationale: The task was to migrate and fix all breaking changes. Response A completed the migration: retargeted to net9.0, fixed the BinaryFormatter, nullable UserAgent, and JsonDocument null-handling issues, and achieved a clean build (0 errors, 0 warnings), despite some patch-format struggles it recovered from. Response B stopped after loading a skill and correctly identifying the BinaryFormatter issue, but blocked asking for a decision rather than completing the task—leaving the migration unfinished and the other two breaking changes unaddressed. While B's caution about cache format is reasonable, replacing BinaryFormatter with System.Text.Json and invalidating cache is the standard expected action, which A performed. A delivered a working result; B did not.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: App with empty environment variables, ZIP encoding, and keyed DI services
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses applied the same three core fixes and reached a clean net9.0 build. The key differentiator is that Response A gave up on producing a runnable app and built the sources as a library (via -p:OutputType=Library override), effectively masking the missing entry point rather than resolving it. Response B properly wired a minimal ASP.NET Core host with a Program.cs and made Startup.Configure public, producing an actual buildable executable web app and also ran tests. B's approach was more methodical (used the migration skill, consulted reference docs) and more complete. Neither response explicitly articulated the underlying .NET 9 breaking-change mechanics the rubric describes, so per-criterion they tie, but B delivers a genuinely better final result.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: CI pipeline with Terminal Logger parsing and version constraints
judgeRationales.rationale: B is stronger primarily because it correctly identifies and addresses the Terminal Logger output-format issue (a key rubric item) and provides a more robust architecture separating a root global.json pinned to SDK 8 (preserving VS 17.11 and dotnet watch net8.0 compatibility) from a .ci/global.json pinned to SDK 9. This directly satisfies the constraint that developers use VS 17.11 and net8.0 watch while CI migrates to .NET 9. A instead pinned the single global.json to SDK 9.0.100, which would break VS 17.11 developers and dotnet watch—a real functional problem A only partially acknowledges as an upgrade requirement. A does slightly better on the netstandard1.x warning by empirically hitting NETSDK1215, but B's overall correctness and coverage of Terminal Logger make it the better result. Both miss the workload format and Hot Reload rubric items.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Containerized app with env var precedence reversal and zlib removal
judgeRationales.rationale: The critical technical distinction in this task is that DOTNET_ThreadPool_MinThreads is not a supported runtime knob in .NET 9 and does NOT override runtimeconfig.json (so MinThreads stays 25), while the GC env vars DO take precedence. Response A correctly identifies this subtlety, stating the env var is ignored and would leave 25 — though it undercuts itself by then claiming runtime config sets 4. Response B gets this wrong entirely, asserting the effective value becomes 4. Both handle the GC precedence and zlib/SkiaSharp points equally well, and neither gives strong remediation guidance. A's correct handling of the hardest criterion makes it slightly better overall despite its internal inconsistency.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Containerized app with zlib dependency and runtime configuration
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses cover zlib, GC precedence, Monitor tags, and global.json, and critically BOTH fail the most important trap: neither identifies that DOTNET_ThreadPool_MinThreads is not a supported runtime configuration environment variable and therefore has no effect (both wrongly claim it applies). Given the tie on that key criterion, the deciding factors are thoroughness and precision. Response A actually built the Docker image with .NET 9, verified the monitor:9.0 tag via manifest inspect, confirmed zlib in the image, pinned an accurate SDK version, and gave concrete Monitor tag examples. Response B leaned on the skill but ran a real build reaching CS5001 and was more concise but less precise on GC precedence and Monitor tags. A is slightly better overall due to greater verification and specificity, though both share the same critical omission.

Response A also lists more comprehensive EF9 Cosmos breaking changes. This gives A a slight overall edge."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Library with String.Trim span overload, keyed services, and InlineArray
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identified and fixed all four breaking changes and achieved a clean build with zero warnings/errors. The core outcomes are essentially equivalent. A slight edge to A: A also enabled nullable analysis and its csproj is a clean net9.0 target. B added a FrameworkReference to Microsoft.AspNetCore.App, which was needed to make the ASP.NET types (FromKeyedServices) resolve—though in this stripped-down repro it's arguably reasonable. However, the code compiles after removing the attribute anyway, so the added framework reference is somewhat superfluous given the file no longer uses ASP.NET types. Both are strong; the gap is small. A's approach was also more methodical (grounding fixes in the actual Microsoft breaking-change docs via web_fetch) whereas B relied on a skill. Overall roughly equal with a marginal lean to A.

B also leveraged the migration skill methodically. This makes B slightly better overall despite similar core outcomes.
